claims.source: The fact that strong ced-3(lf) alleles cause robust defects in programmed cell death but not the developmental defects described above suggests that the functions of ced-3 with miRISCs uncovered in our screen are non-apoptotic.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of known apoptotic phenotypes with the novel developmental phenotypes observed in this study.

claims.claim: The functions of ced-3 with miRISCs uncovered in this screen are non-apoptotic.
claims.source: The fact that strong ced-3(lf) alleles cause robust defects in programmed cell death but not the developmental defects described above suggests that the functions of ced-3 with miRISCs uncovered in our screen are non-apoptotic.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ced-3(lf) alone does not cause the developmental defects seen in double mutants.

claims.claim: ain-1(lf) mutation did not enhance the apoptotic defect of ced-3(rf) animals as assayed by observing the perdurance of lin-11::GFP positive undead P9-11.aap cells.
claims.source: We found that, in contrast to the positive control, mcd-1(lf), the ain-1(lf) mutation did not enhance the apoptotic defect of ced-3(rf) animals as assayed by observing the perdurance of lin-11::GFP positive undead P9-11.aap cells (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: ain-1(lf) mutation did not enhance any subtle nuc-1(lf) phenotype.
claims.source: Because nuc-1 encodes an effector nuclease important for the proper execution of apoptosis (Wu et al., 2000), we then tested if the ain-1(lf) mutation was able to enhance any subtle nuc-1(lf) phenotype and found no significant defect beyond the phenotypes of the single mutants (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 3C and cites previous work on nuc-1 function.

claims.claim: ain-1(RNAi) did not affect the number of apoptotic cell corpses accumulating in the heads of ced-1(lf) first stage larvae.
claims.source: Finally, ain-1(RNAi) did not affect the number of apoptotic cell corpses accumulating in the heads of ced-1(lf) first stage larvae (Figure 3D), which are defective in cell corpse engulfment allowing for visualization of dead cell corpses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell corpse counting data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The ain-1 and ced-3 interaction is non-apoptotic.
claims.source: Therefore, the ain-1 and ced-3 interaction described above is non-apoptotic.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple apoptotic assays showing no enhancement by ain-1(lf).

claims.claim: ced-3(lf) and ced-4(lf) single mutants have mild reduction in their rates of post-embryonic growth similar to the ain-1(lf) and alg-1(lf) mutants.
claims.source: Further analysis indicated that the ced-3(lf) and ced-4(lf) single mutants have mild reduction in their rates of post-embryonic growth similar to the ain-1(lf) and alg-1(lf) mutants (Figure 4A–C and also Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for more ced-3(lf) data).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) and ced-3(lf);alg-1(lf) double mutants, but not ced-3(lf);ain-2(lf), have significantly slower growth rates beyond either single mutant.
claims.source: Additionally, the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) and ced-3(lf);alg-1(lf) double mutants, but not ced-3(lf);ain-2(lf), have significantly slower growth rates beyond either single mutant (Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting cooperativity in regulating the related developmental programs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by developmental timing data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: Mutations in the let-7-family members, mir-48 and mir-84, had the strongest effect with a fully penetrant egg-laying defect observed in the ced-3(lf);mir-48(lf);mir-84(lf) triple mutant.
claims.source: Specifically, mutations in the let-7-family members, mir-48 and mir-84, had the strongest effect with a fully penetrant egg-laying defect observed in the ced-3(lf);mir-48(lf);mir-84(lf) triple mutant (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic data from miRNA deletion mutants shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The ced-3(lf);mir-1(lf);mir-84(lf) triple mutant displayed some developmental defects not seen in the mir-1(lf);mir-84(lf), ced-3(lf);mir-1(lf), or the ced-3(lf);mir-84(lf) double mutants.
claims.source: Interestingly, the ced-3(lf);mir-1(lf);mir-84(lf) triple mutant displayed some developmental defects not seen in the mir-1(lf);mir-84(lf), ced-3(lf);mir-1(lf), or the ced-3(lf);mir-84(lf) double mutants (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: ced-3(lf) significantly enhanced adult alae defects in miR-48(lf),miR-84(lf);ced-3(lf) triple mutant and the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutant, but not the ced-3(lf);mir-1(lf);mir-84(lf) triple mutant.
claims.source: We found that ced-3(lf) significantly enhanced adult alae defects (Figure 5C,D). This effect was observed for both the miR-48(lf),miR-84(lf);ced-3(lf) triple mutant and the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutant, but not the ced-3(lf);mir-1(lf);mir-84(lf) triple mutant (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by adult alae phenotypic data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claims.claim: The expression of some developmental timing regulators is co-regulated by miRISCs and ced-3.
claims.source: These findings suggested the hypothesis that the expression of some developmental timing regulators is co-regulated by miRISCs and ced-3.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from the genetic interaction data with miRNAs and temporal cell fate patterning defects.

claims.claim: Wild-type animals consistently have 16 seam cells on both the left and right sides by adulthood.
claims.source: Wild-type animals consistently have 16 seam cells on both the left and right sides by adulthood (Joshi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Joshi et al., 2010).

claims.claim: LIN-14 is highly expressed during L1 to promote L1-specific developmental programs.
claims.source: LIN-14 is highly expressed during L1 to promote L1-specific developmental programs, whereas LIN-28 is highly expressed from late embryonic to L2 stages and acts to promote the L2-specific programs including the only normal symmetric division of V1–V4 and V6 seam cells (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984; Ambros, 1989; Ruvkun and Giusto, 1989; Moss et al., 1997; Rougvie and Moss, 2013)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on LIN-14 function.

claims.claim: LIN-28 is highly expressed from late embryonic to L2 stages and acts to promote the L2-specific programs including the only normal symmetric division of V1–V4 and V6 seam cells.
claims.source: LIN-14 is highly expressed during L1 to promote L1-specific developmental programs, whereas LIN-28 is highly expressed from late embryonic to L2 stages and acts to promote the L2-specific programs including the only normal symmetric division of V1–V4 and V6 seam cells (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984; Ambros, 1989; Ruvkun and Giusto, 1989; Moss et al., 1997; Rougvie and Moss, 2013)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on LIN-28 function.

claims.claim: Expression of LIN-14 and LIN-28 rapidly diminishes after L1 and L2, respectively, which is necessary for animals to progress to the next stage.
claims.source: Expression of LIN-14 and LIN-28 rapidly diminishes after L1 and L2, respectively, which is necessary for animals to progress to the next stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of developmental timing and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Loss-of-function mutations in lin-14 and lin-28 result in animals skipping the L1- and L2-specific programs, respectively (precocious phenotype).
claims.source: Loss-of-function (lf) mutations in lin-14 and lin-28 result in animals skipping the L1- and L2-specific programs, respectively (precocious phenotype) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of heterochronic mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: Hyperactive (gain-of-function, gf) mutations leading to prolonged expression of lin-14 or lin-28 cause the animals to reiterate the corresponding stage (retarded phenotype).
claims.source: In contrast, hyperactive (gain-of-function, gf) mutations leading to prolonged expression of each gene cause the animals to reiterate the corresponding stage (retarded phenotype) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of heterochronic mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: Mammalian DIS3L2 is the ribonuclease that degrades the uridylated pre-let-7 miRNA following binding by LIN-28 and 3′-oligo-uridylation by a polyU polymerase.
claims.source: Mammalian DIS3L2 was recently annotated as the ribonuclease that degrades the uridylated pre-let-7 miRNA following binding by LIN-28 and 3′-oligo-uridylation by a polyU polymerase (Chang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent work (Chang et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The C. elegans gene F48E8.6 is the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian Dis3l2.
claims.source: We identified the likely C. elegans ortholog of Dis3l2 and named it disl-2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment and domain prediction shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The ain-1(lf) mutant alone has a mild increase in the number of seam cells by late larval development.
claims.source: As previously published (Ding et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2007), we also found that the ain-1(lf) mutant alone has a mild increase in the number of seam cells by late larval development (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by seam cell counting data and cites previous publications.

claims.claim: The ced-3(lf) mutant alone rarely shows altered seam cell numbers.
claims.source: As previously published (Ding et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2007), we also found that the ain-1(lf) mutant alone has a mild increase in the number of seam cells by late larval development (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2) consistent with the well-established role of miRNAs in regulation of temporal cell fate patterning; whereas the ced-3(lf) mutant alone rarely shows altered seam cell numbers (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by seam cell counting data shown in Figure 6A-B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants have both a markedly increased number of seam cells and an increased range of seam cell number by late larval development with a mean value (±SD) of 25.9 (±5.5) per side.
claims.source: Strikingly, the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants have both a markedly increased number of seam cells and an increased range of seam cell number by late larval development (Figure 6A,B) with a mean value (±SD) of 25.9 (±5.5) per side.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative seam cell counting data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: The ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants hatch with the correct number of seam cells but they continue to increase inappropriately throughout later larval development.
claims.source: Notably, the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants hatch with the correct number of seam cells but they continue to increase inappropriately throughout later larval development (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by seam cell counting at different developmental stages shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: The increased number of seam cells in the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants was partially suppressed by down-regulating lin-14, lin-28, or disl-2 through RNAi treatment beginning at L2.
claims.source: We found that the increased number of seam cells in the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants was partially suppressed by down-regulating lin-14, lin-28, or disl-2(Dis3l2) through RNAi treatment beginning at L2 (Figure 6C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi suppression data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: An abnormally high level of lin-14, lin-28, or disl-2 could be a significant contributor to the seam cell phenotype in ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants.
claims.source: We found that the increased number of seam cells in the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants was partially suppressed by down-regulating lin-14, lin-28, or disl-2(Dis3l2) through RNAi treatment beginning at L2 (Figure 6C), suggesting that an abnormally high level of any of the three proteins could be a significant contributor to the phenotype.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the RNAi suppression results.

claims.claim: ced-3(lf) enhanced the heterochronic defect of lin-66 reduction.
claims.source: Consistent with a ced-3 function in lin-28-mediated temporal cell fate patterning regulation, we also observed that ced-3(lf) enhanced the heterochronic defect of lin-66 reduction (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Down-regulation of lin-14, lin-28, or disl-2 by RNAi beginning at L2 could significantly suppress the defects in the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants.
claims.source: We further found that down-regulation of lin-14, lin-28, or disl-2(Dis3l2) by RNAi beginning at L2 could significantly suppress the defects in the ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi suppression data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: ced-3 cooperates with miRNAs to regulate the lin-14-lin-28-disl-2(Dis3l2) axis during development.
claims.source: These findings suggest that ced-3 cooperates with miRNAs to regulate the lin-14-lin-28-disl-2(Dis3l2) axis during development.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction and suppression data.

claims.claim: LIN-14, LIN-28, and DISL-2 contain multiple consensus CED-3 cleavage sites that consist of a tetra-peptide sequence usually ending in an aspartic acid residue.
claims.source: As a caspase, we thought that CED-3 may directly repress the expression of these genes through proteolytic cleavage, which is consistent with our observation that LIN-14, LIN-28, and DISL-2 contain multiple consensus CED-3 cleavage sites that consist of a tetra-peptide sequence usually ending in an aspartic acid residue (Xue et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and cites previous work on CED-3 cleavage specificity.

claims.claim: DISL-2 was robustly cleaved by the CED-3 caspase in vitro.
claims.source: We found that the DIS3L2 ribonuclease homolog, DISL-2, was robustly cleaved by the CED-3 caspase while LIN-14 and LIN-28 were partially cleaved (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: LIN-14 and LIN-28 were partially cleaved by CED-3 in vitro.
claims.source: We found that the DIS3L2 ribonuclease homolog, DISL-2, was robustly cleaved by the CED-3 caspase while LIN-14 and LIN-28 were partially cleaved (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The partial LIN-28 cleavage by CED-3 was completely blocked by addition of the caspase-specific-inhibitor zDEVD-fmk.
claims.source: We further tested the specificity of the partial LIN-28 cleavage by CED-3 and found that it was completely blocked by addition of the caspase-specific-inhibitor zDEVD-fmk (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assay with inhibitor shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Mutating the second aspartic acid residue to an alanine (D31A) in the DVVD sequence entirely eliminated CED-3 cleavage of LIN-28.
claims.source: The identified sequence DVVD fits the canonical CED-3 recognition motif (DxxD) (Xue et al., 1996) and mutating the second aspartic acid residue to an alanine (D31A in Figure 7D) entirely eliminated CED-3 cleavage.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: CED-3 proteolysis of LIN-28A generates an N-terminal asparagine in the remaining protein.
claims.source: CED-3 proteolysis of LIN-28A generates an N-terminal asparagine in the remaining protein (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the cleavage site determination and illustrated in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Asparagine is known to function generally as a destabilizing residue at the N-terminus of eukaryotic proteins resulting in proteasomal degradation in a phenomenon termed the N-end rule.
claims.source: Asparagine is known to function generally as a destabilizing residue at the N-terminus of eukaryotic proteins resulting in proteasomal degradation in a phenomenon termed the N-end rule (Sriram et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on the N-end rule (Sriram et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The dynamic decrease in LIN-28 abundance during L2–L4 stages was similarly delayed by two different ced-3(lf) mutations.
claims.source: We found that the dynamic decrease in LIN-28 abundance during L2–L4 stages was similarly delayed by two different ced-3(lf) mutations (Figure 8A and quantitation shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: At late L4 (48 hr), LIN-28 was almost completely absent in both wild type and ced-3(lf) mutants, indicating the role of general, non-CED-3-mediated, proteolysis during late larval stages.
claims.source: At late L4 (48 hr in Figure 8A), LIN-28 was almost completely absent in both wild type and ced-3(lf) mutants, indicating the role of general, non-CED-3-mediated, proteolysis during late larval stages.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from Western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: The 22-kDa cleavage product observed in the in vitro assay was not observable in vivo, consistent with the idea that the cleavage product with an asparagine at its N-terminus was possibly degraded by an additional proteolytic process.
claims.source: Interestingly, the 22-kDa cleavage product observed in the in vitro assay (Figure 7D,E) was not observable in vivo (Figure 8A), consistent with the idea that the cleavage product with an asparagine at its N-terminus was possibly degraded by an additional proteolytic process.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of in vitro and in vivo data.

claims.claim: The ced-3(lf) mutation delayed the proper down-regulation of the LIN-28::GFP reporter at L3 in the hypodermis.
claims.source: We observed that the ced-3(lf) mutation delayed the proper down-regulation of the LIN-28::GFP reporter at L3 in the hypodermis (Figure 8B–D and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8B-D and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-C.

claims.claim: Down-regulation of LIN-28::GFP expression was delayed in neuronal cells in the head in ced-3(lf) mutants.
claims.source: We also found that down-regulation of LIN-28::GFP expression was delayed in neuronal cells in the head (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D-E.

claims.claim: The lin-28(D31A)::gfp transgene was able to rescue the Pvl phenotype in lin-28(n719,lf) animals.
claims.source: To ensure that the LIN-28(D31A) mutation did not disrupt the global function of the protein, we tested its ability to overcome the highly penetrant protruding vulva (Pvl) phenotype in lin-28(n719,lf) animals and found that it was able to rescue the Pvl phenotype (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The copy number of the lin-28(D31A)::gfp transgene is slightly lower than that of the non-mutated lin-28(+)::gfp transgene.
claims.source: Following integration and outcrossing, we found the copy number of the lin-28(D31A)::gfp transgene to be slightly lower than that of the non-mutated lin-28(+)::gfp transgene (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The lin-28(D31A)::gfp transgene alone caused a delay in larval development similar to that caused by the combination of the lin-28(+)::gfp transgene with ced-3(lf).
claims.source: We then examined the developmental profile and found that the lin-28(D31A)::gfp transgene alone caused a delay in larval development similar to that caused by the combination of the lin-28(+)::gfp transgene with ced-3(lf) (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The lin-28(D31A)::gfp integration had less basal expression than the non-mutated lin-28(+)::gfp integration.
claims.source: Western blot analysis showed that the lin-28(D31A)::gfp integration had less basal expression than the non-mutated lin-28(+)::gfp integration, consistent with the lower copy number estimate.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data and is consistent with copy number data.

claims.claim: A quantifiable difference in the down-regulation of the lin-28(D31A)::gfp transgene compared to the lin-28(+)::gfp transgene was observed.
claims.source: We observed a quantifiable difference in the down-regulation of the lin-28(D31A)::gfp transgene compared to the lin-28(+)::gfp transgene (Figure 9B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9B-C.

claims.claim: A failure in CED-3 cleavage of LIN-28 leads to slower degradation of LIN-28 and is one of the causes of slower development.
claims.source: This finding provides evidence that a failure in CED-3 cleavage of LIN-28 leads to slower degradation of LIN-28 and is one of the causes of slower development, since the D31A point mutation alone resulted in both a slower growth rate (Figure 9A) and delayed LIN-28 down-regulation (Figure 9B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the D31A mutant phenotypic data.

claims.claim: Disrupting CED-3 activity on LIN-28 enhances adult alae defects.
claims.source: To further test the functional outcome of both the LIN-28(D31A) transgene and the LIN-28(+) transgene combined with ced-3(lf), we examined the adult-specific alae and found significant defects including low quality and gapped alae (Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by adult alae phenotypic data shown in Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The LIN-14::GFP level was modestly increased in ced-3(lf) mutants in vivo at the L1 stage.
claims.source: Consistent with LIN-14 being modestly cleaved by CED-3 in vitro (Figure 7A), we found that the LIN-14::GFP level was modestly increased in ced-3(lf) mutants in vivo at the L1 stage (Figure 9—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: CED-3 caspase has a non-apoptotic function that regulates multiple developmental events through proteolytic inactivation.
claims.source: We provide evidence for a non-apoptotic function of CED-3 caspase that regulates multiple developmental events through proteolytic inactivation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: CED-3 cleaves LIN-14, LIN-28, and DISL-2 proteins in vitro.
claims.source: Specifically, LIN-14, LIN-28, and DISL-2 proteins are known miRNA targets, key regulators of developmental timing, and/or stem cell pluripotency factors involved in miRNA processing. We show CED-3 cleaves these proteins in vitro.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data.

claims.claim: CED-3 down-regulates LIN-28 in vivo, possibly rendering it more susceptible to proteasomal degradation.
claims.source: We also show CED-3 down-regulates LIN-28 in vivo, possibly rendering it more susceptible to proteasomal degradation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo Western blot and fluorescence data, with speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: The CED-3 mechanism may critically contribute to the robustness of gene expression dynamics governing proper developmental control.
claims.source: This mechanism may critically contribute to the robustness of gene expression dynamics governing proper developmental control.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative conclusion based on the overall findings.

claims.claim: miRNAs mostly exert repression of gene expression by blocking target mRNA translation and/or through mRNA decay as part of the miRNA-induced-silencing complex (miRISC), which includes GW182 and argonaute proteins.
claims.source: miRNAs mostly exert repression of gene expression by blocking target mRNA translation and/or through mRNA decay as part of the miRNA-induced-silencing complex (miRISC), which includes GW182 and argonaute proteins (Ding and Han, 2007; Fabian and Sonenberg, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on miRNA mechanisms.

claims.claim: miRNA-mediated gene silencing is a critical regulatory mechanism that ensures dynamic changes in gene expression during animal development or other physiological processes.
claims.source: miRNA-mediated gene silencing is a critical regulatory mechanism that ensures dynamic changes in gene expression during animal development or other physiological processes (Ambros, 2004; Bartel and Chen, 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on miRNA functions.

claims.claim: Specific physiological roles of individual miRNAs are often executed through the combinatory effects of multi-miRNA, multi-target mRNA networks.
claims.source: However, specific physiological roles of individual miRNAs are often executed through the combinatory effects of multi-miRNA, multi-target mRNA networks (Brenner et al., 2010; Karp et al., 2011; Kudlow et al., 2012; Miska et al., 2007; Parry et al., 2007; Than et al., 2013; Alvarez-Saavedra and Horvitz, 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on miRNA networks.

claims.claim: miRNA–mRNA interaction networks may act in concert, and often semi-redundantly, with other regulatory mechanisms to limit the expression of many genes involved in animal development or other physiological functions.
claims.source: Moreover, these miRNA–mRNA interaction networks may act in concert, and often semi-redundantly, with other regulatory mechanisms to limit the expression of many genes involved in animal development or other physiological functions (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The ain-1(lf) mutant has a mild heterochronic phenotype.
claims.source: While the ain-1(lf) mutant has a mild heterochronic phenotype and the ain-2(lf) mutant is superficially wild-type, loss of both genes results in severe pleiotropic defects including alteration in temporal cell fate patterning.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ain-1 mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: The ain-2(lf) mutant is superficially wild-type.
claims.source: While the ain-1(lf) mutant has a mild heterochronic phenotype and the ain-2(lf) mutant is superficially wild-type, loss of both genes results in severe pleiotropic defects including alteration in temporal cell fate patterning.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ain-2 mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: Loss of both ain-1 and ain-2 genes results in severe pleiotropic defects including alteration in temporal cell fate patterning.
claims.source: While the ain-1(lf) mutant has a mild heterochronic phenotype and the ain-2(lf) mutant is superficially wild-type, loss of both genes results in severe pleiotropic defects including alteration in temporal cell fate patterning.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ain-1;ain-2 double mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: CED-3 is capable of cleaving more than 22 C. elegans proteins in an in vitro proteomics survey.
claims.source: Consistent with this, a previous report showed that CED-3 is capable of cleaving more than 22 C. elegans proteins in an in vitro proteomics survey (Taylor et al., 2007)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Taylor et al., 2007).

claims.claim: ced-3 may play important roles in neural regeneration.
claims.source: Consistent with this, a previous report showed that CED-3 is capable of cleaving more than 22 C. elegans proteins in an in vitro proteomics survey (Taylor et al., 2007) and two recent genetics-based findings showed that ced-3 may play important roles in neural regeneration (Pinan-Lucarre et al., 2012) and aging (Yee et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent work (Pinan-Lucarre et al., 2012).

claims.claim: ced-3 may play important roles in aging.
claims.source: Consistent with this, a previous report showed that CED-3 is capable of cleaving more than 22 C. elegans proteins in an in vitro proteomics survey (Taylor et al., 2007) and two recent genetics-based findings showed that ced-3 may play important roles in neural regeneration (Pinan-Lucarre et al., 2012) and aging (Yee et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent work (Yee et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The described CED-3 function in repressing gene expression is likely in contrast to the role of CED-3 in promoting apoptosis through activation of protein targets by cleavage at specific sites.
claims.source: Second, the described CED-3 function in repressing gene expression is likely in contrast to the role of CED-3 in promoting apoptosis through activation of protein targets by cleavage at specific sites (Nakagawa et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison with known apoptotic functions of CED-3 cited from previous work.

claims.claim: CED-3 cleavage alone may already destroy the target protein activity.
claims.source: Here, the CED-3 cleavage alone may already destroy the target protein activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative based on the observed cleavage patterns.

claims.claim: The cleavage products may be further degraded by other degradation systems notably via N-terminal destabilizing residues which may make the target more susceptible to additional degradation mechanisms, such as proteasomal degradation.
claims.source: Additionally, the cleavage products may be further degraded by other degradation systems notably via N-terminal destabilizing residues which may make the target more susceptible to additional degradation mechanisms, such as proteasomal degradation (Sriram et al., 2011) (Figure 10B).

claims.claim: The CED-3 function operates continually during development to facilitate rapid turnover of regulatory proteins at the post-translational level and in cooperation with other regulatory mechanisms.
claims.source: We hypothesize that this function operates continually during development to facilitate rapid turnover of these regulatory proteins at the post-translational level and in cooperation with other regulatory mechanisms (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the overall findings.

results.result: A genome-wide RNAi screen identified 126 genetic interactors with miRISC components ain-1 and ain-2, of which 118 are novel. The interactors show enrichment for protein stability genes and differential pleiotropism between ain-1 and ain-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are well-supported by the double-blind RNAi screen methodology and quantitative data presented in Figure 1. The screen design, confirmation strategy, and gene ontology analysis provide converging evidence for the identification and characterization of these interactors.

results.result: Loss of ced-3 caspase genetically interacts with ain-1 (but not ain-2) to produce pleiotropic developmental defects. This interaction is also observed with other miRISC components and cell death pathway genes, with the intestine and hypodermis being major sites of function.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C13 are supported by extensive phenotypic characterization using multiple alleles (C7-C10), tissue-specific rescue experiments (C11-C12), and appropriate citations for ced-3 cell autonomy (C13). The specificity of the ain-1 but not ain-2 interaction (C9) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: The ced-3 and ain-1 genetic interaction is non-apoptotic, as demonstrated by multiple independent apoptotic assays showing no enhancement of cell death phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 are well-supported by three independent apoptotic assays (C16-C18) that all show negative results, combined with the observation that strong ced-3(lf) alleles cause apoptotic but not developmental defects (C14). The convergence of multiple negative controls strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: ced-3(lf) and ced-4(lf) single mutants show mild growth delays similar to ain-1(lf) and alg-1(lf), and ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) and ced-3(lf);alg-1(lf) double mutants show synergistic growth delays.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21 are supported by developmental timing data across multiple time points (Figure 4A-C and supplements). The observation of synergistic effects in double mutants but not with ain-2 provides specificity.

results.result: Specific miRNA deletions (particularly let-7 family members mir-48 and mir-84) show genetic interactions with ced-3(lf), producing developmental defects and enhanced adult alae defects, suggesting co-regulation of developmental timing regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are supported by systematic screening of miRNA deletion mutants and quantitative phenotypic analysis (Figure 5). The specificity of effects with different miRNA combinations and the adult alae phenotypes provide converging evidence. C25 is appropriately stated as a hypothesis.

results.result: Background knowledge on C. elegans developmental timing: wild-type seam cell numbers, LIN-14 and LIN-28 expression patterns and functions, and mammalian DIS3L2 function in pre-let-7 degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 are appropriately cited to established literature and provide necessary background context. These are well-established facts in the field supported by multiple citations.

results.result: The C. elegans gene F48E8.6 (named disl-2) is the ortholog of mammalian Dis3l2.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by sequence alignment and domain prediction analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1, demonstrating conserved catalytic domains and ribonuclease II family signature.

results.result: ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants show a dramatic increase in seam cell numbers (mean 25.9±5.5 per side) compared to single mutants, with normal numbers at hatching but inappropriate increases during larval development.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are strongly supported by quantitative seam cell counting data at multiple developmental stages (Figure 6A-B and supplements). The temporal analysis (C37) demonstrates that the defect arises post-embryonically, which is critical for understanding the mechanism.

results.result: RNAi knockdown of lin-14, lin-28, or disl-2 beginning at L2 partially suppresses both the seam cell phenotype and general developmental defects of ced-3(lf);ain-1(lf) double mutants, suggesting ced-3 cooperates with miRNAs to regulate these factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are supported by RNAi suppression experiments (Figure 6C-D). The partial suppression by multiple independent targets provides strong genetic evidence for the proposed regulatory axis. The enhancement of lin-66 defects (C40) provides additional supporting evidence.

results.result: CED-3 cleaves LIN-14, LIN-28, and DISL-2 in vitro, with DISL-2 being robustly cleaved and LIN-28 partially cleaved at a specific DVVD site (D31), generating an N-terminal asparagine.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C49 are well-supported by in vitro cleavage assays with appropriate controls including caspase inhibitor (C46) and site-directed mutagenesis (C48). The identification of the specific cleavage site and resulting N-terminal residue is rigorous.

results.result: Asparagine functions as a destabilizing N-terminal residue leading to proteasomal degradation via the N-end rule.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is appropriately cited to established literature (Sriram et al., 2011) on the N-end rule pathway.

results.result: LIN-28 protein down-regulation during L2-L4 is delayed in ced-3(lf) mutants, with eventual complete degradation by late L4. The 22-kDa cleavage product observed in vitro is not detected in vivo, consistent with rapid degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by Western blot analysis with two independent ced-3(lf) alleles (Figure 8A and supplement). The absence of the cleavage product in vivo (C53) is appropriately interpreted as consistent with N-end rule degradation, though this remains speculative.

results.result: ced-3(lf) delays down-regulation of LIN-28::GFP reporter expression at L3 in both hypodermis and neuronal cells in the head.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by fluorescence microscopy of stage-matched L3 larvae (Figure 8B-D and supplements). The authors appropriately controlled for developmental stage by measuring gonad length, addressing a potential confounding factor.

results.result: A caspase-cleavage-resistant LIN-28(D31A) transgene causes developmental delays and delayed LIN-28 down-regulation similar to ced-3(lf), and enhances adult alae defects, demonstrating that CED-3 cleavage of LIN-28 is functionally important for development.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 are well-supported by multiple complementary experiments: rescue of lin-28(lf) (C56), transgene copy number determination (C57), developmental timing (C58), Western blot analysis (C59-C60), and adult alae phenotypes (C62). This provides strong evidence that the specific cleavage site is functionally relevant in vivo.

results.result: LIN-14::GFP levels are modestly increased in ced-3(lf) mutants at L1 stage.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by Western blot data from three independent experiments (Figure 9—figure supplement 4). The modest effect is consistent with the partial in vitro cleavage observed for LIN-14.

results.result: CED-3 caspase has a non-apoptotic function regulating development through proteolytic inactivation of LIN-14, LIN-28, and DISL-2, potentially enhancing robustness of gene expression dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are well-supported by the cumulative evidence from genetic interactions, in vitro cleavage, and in vivo protein level changes. C67 is appropriately speculative about the broader significance. The integration of multiple lines of evidence (genetic, biochemical, cell biological) strongly supports this major conclusion.

results.result: Background on miRNA mechanisms: miRNAs repress gene expression through miRISC, are critical for development, often function through multi-miRNA networks, and act semi-redundantly with other regulatory mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are appropriately cited to established literature and provide necessary background context for the study.

results.result: Background on ain-1 and ain-2 mutant phenotypes: ain-1(lf) has mild heterochronic phenotype, ain-2(lf) is superficially wild-type, and loss of both causes severe pleiotropic defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are established knowledge appropriately used to justify the screen design.

results.result: Prior work shows CED-3 can cleave >22 C. elegans proteins in vitro and may have roles in neural regeneration and aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are appropriately cited to prior literature and provide context for non-apoptotic CED-3 functions.

results.result: The non-apoptotic CED-3 function described here contrasts with apoptotic functions (protein activation vs. inactivation), may directly destroy target activity, and may facilitate degradation via N-end rule, operating continually during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are largely speculative (C79-C81) or inferential (C78). While the speculation is reasonable and supported by the N-end rule literature (C80), direct evidence for proteasomal involvement and continuous operation during development is limited. The absence of the cleavage product in vivo (C53) is consistent with but does not prove N-end rule degradation.
